title: Ovary
description: Female reproductive organ that produces egg cells
wiki_lead:
The ovary (from Latin  ōvārium 'egg') is the paired primary sex organ, or gonad in the female reproductive system. The ovaries are responsible for the production of oogonia, their development to oocytes (immature egg cells), and the release as a mature egg cell (ovum) at ovulation. The egg cells, or ova are also known as gametes, and the process of their development is gametogenesis, known as oogenesis in the female. During their development each oocyte is surrounded by granulosa cells, forming an ovarian follicle. The ovary progresses through many stages beginning in the prenatal period through menopause.
The ovary also produces hormones, specifically sex hormones (sex steroids) to assist in the development of the egg cells. This hormone production in the granulosa cells of the ovarian follicles,  makes the ovary an endocrine gland as well as a sex organ. The hormones are estrogen, and progesterone that also play an important part in the development and function of the female reproductive organs, and in  the development at puberty of secondary sex characteristics.
The paired ovaries are located one on either side of the uterus, and connect with the uterus through the fallopian tubes. They are held in place by the ovarian ligament, and the suspensory ligament of the ovary.
Many of the structural and functional features of the human ovary are shared with other mammals and vertebrates and ovaries of some kind are found in many invertebrates. This article is primarily about the human ovary.
wiki_fulltext:
The ovary (from Latin  ōvārium 'egg') is the paired primary sex organ, or gonad in the female reproductive system. The ovaries are responsible for the production of oogonia, their development to oocytes (immature egg cells), and the release as a mature egg cell (ovum) at ovulation. The egg cells, or ova are also known as gametes, and the process of their development is gametogenesis, known as oogenesis in the female. During their development each oocyte is surrounded by granulosa cells, forming an ovarian follicle. The ovary progresses through many stages beginning in the prenatal period through menopause.
The ovary also produces hormones, specifically sex hormones (sex steroids) to assist in the development of the egg cells. This hormone production in the granulosa cells of the ovarian follicles,  makes the ovary an endocrine gland as well as a sex organ. The hormones are estrogen, and progesterone that also play an important part in the development and function of the female reproductive organs, and in  the development at puberty of secondary sex characteristics.
The paired ovaries are located one on either side of the uterus, and connect with the uterus through the fallopian tubes. They are held in place by the ovarian ligament, and the suspensory ligament of the ovary.
Many of the structural and functional features of the human ovary are shared with other mammals and vertebrates and ovaries of some kind are found in many invertebrates. This article is primarily about the human ovary.


Structure
At puberty each ovary measures around  3 cm in length by 1.5 cm wide and is 1 cm thick, and sits in a depression in the lateral wall of the pelvic cavity. This depression is called the ovarian fossa and measures around 4 cm x 3 cm x 2 cm. The fossa is bounded above by the external iliac artery and vein, in front by the obliterated umbilical artery, and behind by the ureter. 
The ovaries lie within the peritoneal cavity on either side of the uterus to which they are attached via a fibrous cord called the ovarian ligament. They are tethered to the body wall via the suspensory ligament of the ovary, which is a posterior extension of the broad ligament of the uterus. The part of the broad ligament of the uterus that suspends the ovary is known as the mesovarium.
The ovary has an inner medullary core, and an outer cortical region, and is enclosed by a capsule of dense fibrous tissue the tunica albuginea. A layer of cuboidal epithelium from the visceral peritoneum covers the ovaries as ovarian surface epithelium.
The ovarian medulla  is the highly vascular stromal tissue in the center of the ovary.  Its contents include blood vessels, lymphatic vessels, immune cells, and nerves. 
The ovarian hilum is the hilum in the ovary, formed by  the stroma and attached to the ovarian ligament where the blood vessels, lymphatic vessels  and nerves enter the medulla of the ovary.
It is also the main site of ovarian hilus cells also known as ovarian ovarian Leydig cells.
The ovarian cortex is an ill-defined outer region containing many ovarian follicles at different stages of development. The follicles are surrounded by peripheral  stroma. It can be hard to distinguish between the cortex and medulla, but follicles are usually not found in the medulla.


Rete ovarii

The rete ovarii is an epithelial appendage of the ovary to which it is attached. It has been proposed to be presented as an ovarian organ. Before advanced imaging techniques were available the rete ovarii was overlooked as an insignificant embryonic remnant. It has been shown to be a structure of three distinct regions. Columnar epithelial cells create a tubular region ending in blind tips termed the extraovarian rete (EOR). Pseudocolumnar epithelial cells make up a connecting rete (CR). And squamous epithelial cells branch into an intricate network of thin cords of cells with a diameter of around 1-3 cells, known as the intraovarian rete (IOR). The CR connects the EOR to the IOR. In the region of the hilum the intraovarian rete forms part of the ovarian stroma.
The rete ovarii as a whole is surrounded by smooth muscle actin, a vascular network and various types of macrophage.  Experiments suggest that the rete ovarii is secretory,  sending material to the ovary. 
The size of the regions change with the EOR becoming the largest, and the IOR regressing to the medulla. The distinct regions presented suggest a different function for each. Cells of the rete ovarii may be ciliated or non-ciliated, with dense apical microvilli, and mitochondria. Glycogen, and mucins are also indicated in the extraovarian and connecting regions. Cells of the rete ovarii have been identified in the fetal gonads.


Follicles

During prenatal development in the process of oogenesis – the development of the egg cell, follicles form consisting of primary oocytes surrounded by a layer of follicular cells. The earliest follicles are the primordial follicles that consist of a single layer of  pre-granulosa cells known as follicular cells surrounding a primary oocyte.
The numbers of primordial follicles and primary oocytes, peak at around 7 million by week 20 gestational age. Between then and birth, around 6 million will have been lost leaving just one million remaining at birth. There is further loss until at puberty the number is around 300,000 to 400,000.
The follicles are surrounded by peripheral stromal tissue. A large number of primordial follicles are present at birth of which many will be lost perinatally. Follicles develop to maturity in a process of folliculogenesis that supports the development of the oocyte to the mature egg cell.
At puberty, in the menstrual cycle the primordial follicles become triggered to change to primary follicles, and the follicular cells change to granulosa cells. In the transition from primary follicle to secondary follicle, layers of granulosa cells, and an external covering known as the theca forms. In later stages of the transition the theca organises into an  internal and an external layer.
In the later stages of folliculogenesis the follicles include  granulosa cells of the cumulus oophorus, and its inner layer of corona radiata, the zona pellucida, and the internal and external cell layers of the theca, and follicular fluid. At ovulation the oocyte and surrounding zona pellucida, and corona radiata are released into the peritoneal cavity when the follicle ruptures. 
Rupture can take place when the ovarian outer tissues at the point of contact with the follicle erode. This eroded point of exit for the ruptured follicle contents is known as the ovarian stigma. The released egg cell and corona radiata are swept into the fallopian tube by its fimbriae, and if not fertilized after 28-48 hours they degenerate. The remains of the ruptured follicle form the corpus luteum.


Blood supply

The ovarian artery arises from the abdominal aorta and supplies oxygenated blood to the ovary. The ovarian vein drains deoxygenated blood from the ovary to the inferior vena cava or one of its tributaries. The vessels are located within the suspensory ligament of the ovary.


Development

The ovaries develop in early embryogenesis from the genital ridge (or gonadal ridge), following sexual differentiation. The sex of an organism is determined at the time of fertilization, but differentiation only takes place around six weeks later.
An initially expressed gene in the development of the genitourinary system is WT1 that regulates the formation of the genital ridge (and of the kidneys). In the front half of the genital ridge steroidogenic factor 1 (SF-1) is expressed in the somatic cells,  and acts a transcription factor. SF-1 plays an important role in sexual differentiation in the gonad, and in the functioning of Leydig cells. SF1 is expressed later in the steroidogenic thecal and granulosa cells of the ovarian follicles. SF1 levels are low during embryonic development but increase during adolescence and during follicle maturity. SF1 regulates gene expression in the theca and granulosa cells necessary for the function of the ovary.
At birth the ovaries lie in the lower part of the iliac fossae, with the long axis of the ovary being almost vertical. In early childhood the ovaries continue their descent to reach the ovarian fossae. The neonatal ovaries are between one and 3.6 mm long and together have a weight of 0.3 grams. At six weeks of age the ovaries have doubled in weight. There are also furrows seen in the ovarian surface but these disappear by the third month.


Function

The ovaries are the site of oogenesis and function to produce, develop and release the oocytes at ovulation for possible fertilisation. The ovary also produces hormones to assist in this process. The oocytes develop and mature to secondary oocytes in ovarian follicles. Each primordial follicle contains an oocyte surrounded by a single layer of pre-granulosa cells. At puberty, when the primordial follicle changes to a primary follicle, other layers of granulosa cells surround the follicle and become enclosed in a connective tissue covering called the theca. The follicles typically develop one at a time. As they develop they fill with follicular fluid which marks the secondary oocyte stage. When the fluid fills the antrum they are known as antral follicles, that may develop into pre-ovulatory follicles. Most antral follicles undergo atresia with only a few progressing to the pre-ovulatory stage.
At puberty, the ovary begins to secrete increasing levels of hormones. Secondary sex characteristics begin to develop in response to the hormones. The ovary changes structure and function beginning at puberty. Since the ovaries can regulate hormones, they also play an important role in pregnancy and fertility. Usually, ovulation occurs in one of the two ovaries, releasing an egg cell each menstrual cycle. When an egg cell (secondary oocyte) is released and swept into the fallopian tube, feedback mechanisms stimulate the endocrine system, which causes hormone levels to change. These feedback mechanisms are controlled by the hypothalamus and pituitary glands. Messages or signals from the hypothalamus are sent to the pituitary gland. In turn, the pituitary gland releases hormones to the ovaries. From this signaling, the ovaries release their own hormones.
On maturing, a surge of luteinizing hormone is secreted by the pituitary gland, which stimulates the release of the oocyte through the rupture of the follicle, a process called ovulation. The remaining granulosa cells and theca cells from the ruptured follicle reorganize into the corpus luteum, which secretes progesterone to prepare the uterus for an eventual implantation of the embryo.
At maturity, ovaries secrete estrogen, androgen, inhibin, and progestogen. In women before menopause, 50% of testosterone is produced by the ovaries and released directly into the blood stream. The other 50% of testosterone in the bloodstream is made from the conversion of the adrenal pre-androgens (DHEA and androstenedione) to testosterone in other parts of the body. Estrogen is responsible for the appearance of secondary sex characteristics for females at puberty and for the maturation and maintenance of the reproductive organs in their mature functional state. Progesterone prepares the uterus for pregnancy and the mammary glands for lactation. Progesterone functions with estrogen by promoting menstrual cycle changes in the endometrium.


Ovarian aging

At the fourth month of fetal life, follicles number between 6 and 7 million. At birth, the number of follicles has declined to between one and two million, and at puberty the number is decreased to 300,000–400,000. During the reproductive years these follicles undergo atresia at the rate of 1,000 a month, and at menopause the final stage of ovarian aging the ovaries are left with approximately 1000 follicles. Below this threshold regular ovarian cycles cannot be maintained.

grok_lead: The ovary is one of a pair of almond-shaped female gonads located in the pelvic cavity, serving as the primary reproductive organs responsible for producing ova (eggs) and secreting key hormones that regulate the menstrual cycle, fertility, and secondary sexual characteristics. In human anatomy, each ovary measures approximately 3.5 cm in length, 2 cm in width, and 1 cm in thickness, resembling a large olive, and is positioned in the ovarian fossa on either side of the uterus within the broad ligament of the peritoneum. The organ consists of an outer cortex containing ovarian folliclesâstructures that house developing oocytesâand an inner medulla composed of loose connective tissue, blood vessels, lymphatics, and nerves, all enclosed by a thin germinal epithelium and a fibrous tunica albuginea capsule. The ovaries are suspended by peritoneal ligaments, including the ovarian ligament and suspensory ligament, which also facilitate their connection to the fallopian tubes for ovum transport during ovulation. Functionally, the ovaries play a central role in oogenesis, the process of egg maturation, where primordial follicles develop monthly under hormonal influence, culminating in the release of a mature oocyte during ovulation triggered by a luteinizing hormone surge. They also function as endocrine glands, primarily producing estrogen (from granulosa cells in follicles) and progesterone (from the corpus luteum post- ovulation), with smaller amounts of testosterone and inhibin, all regulated by the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis to maintain reproductive health and influence traits such as breast development, body shape, and bone density. Throughout a woman's life, ovarian function evolves: the pool of primordial follicles reaches its maximum during fetal development and subsequently declines throughout life, ovulation occurs cyclically from puberty to menopause, and post- menopause, the ovaries atrophy, reducing hormone output and increasing risks for conditions like osteoporosis.
